subject: Communication
title: Ekman's Six Universal Emotions
description: A short lesson to help you apply Ekman's Six Universal Emotions.

hook.text: Paul Ekman showed photos of faces to an isolated Papua New Guinea tribe. They recognized every emotion.

buildup.text: Six emotions produce universal facial expressions: happiness, sadness, anger, fear, surprise, and disgust.

discovery.text: Each emotion activates specific muscle combinations called 'action units' — measurable and consistent.

twist.text: A real smile uses the orbicularis oculi muscle around the eyes. A fake smile only moves the mouth.

climax.text: Ekman's Facial Action Coding System (FACS) maps every possible muscle movement in the human face.

punchline.text: Six emotions. One face. Every human on Earth.

quiz.question: Which muscle distinguishes a genuine smile from a fake one?

details.summary: Paul Ekman identified six facial expressions recognized across cultures: happiness, sadness, anger, fear, surprise, and disgust. His cross-cultural research suggested these expressions are biologically wired, not learned.
details.whyItMatters: If certain expressions are universal, they provide a shared emotional vocabulary that transcends language barriers and aids cross-cultural understanding.
takeaways: Ekman proposed six universally recognized facial expressions
Cross-cultural studies supported biological origins of emotion
Recent research debates whether recognition is truly universal

faq.question: Have Ekman's six universal emotions been challenged?
faq.answer: Yes. Lisa Feldman Barrett and others argue that emotion categories are culturally constructed and that facial expressions vary more than Ekman claimed. The debate continues between basic emotion theorists and constructionists.

faq.question: Why are these six emotions considered universal?
faq.answer: Ekman showed photographs to isolated tribes in Papua New Guinea who had minimal contact with Western media. They identified the same expressions as people worldwide, suggesting biology rather than culture drives recognition.
